newsitem.title: CANADA: No spending cuts for Canada's violent offenders.
newsitem.headline: No spending cuts for Canada's violent offenders.

text.p: While Canadians wrestled last year with heavy taxes, high unemployment and record household debt, the government spent more on inmates in federal prisons, a government agency said on Tuesday.

Federal inmates saw the amount spent on their upkeep rise four percent -- two percent after inflation -- to C$46,250 ($33,771) per inmate in 1995-96, the government statistics agency, Statistics Canada, said.
Total federal spending on Canada's prisons was C$949 million ($692.9 million) in 1995-96.
Statistics Canada also said the number of inmates in federal prisons stabilized last year for the first time since 1993, with 24,305 people behind bars or on community supervision in 1995-96.
Elsie Wayne, a member of parliament for the opposition Conservative Party, she she did not understand why more was spent to house about the same number of inmates as in 1995.
"It doesn't make sense," Wayne said. "What they're saying to Canadians is 'Break the law and we'll make sure you live in luxury'."
Jacques Belanger, spokesman for the Correctional Service of Canada, denied times were good in Canada's prisons.
More money was being spent because there was a need to build new prisons, Belanger said.
"We also have more and more inmates with a drug-related problem. We have more inmates who are illiterate. So we put an emphasis on counseling."
Criminal justice has become a sore spot for Canada's Liberal government. During the past year, critics have roasted Justice Minister Allan Rock for what they see as a lax attitude toward crime.
Rock's refusal to eliminate a regulation known as the "faint hope clause," which allows convicted murderers to apply for parole after serving 15 years, has particularly angered some Canadians.
